author: Novatian
occasion: Novatian writes because some Christians defend attending public spectacles by appealing to Scripture, and he fears that wounds poorly bound may break open again; he aims to admonish those already instructed rather than instruct them anew.
argument: Novatian argues that Christians must not attend public spectacles because all such shows originate in idolatry, the mother of all games, and were invented by the devil. He refutes appeals to biblical examples such as Elijah, David, and the unnamed apostle by showing these were written to stir virtue, not to permit spectacles. He describes the immorality of the circus, theater, and athletic contests, urging that even apart from idolatry they are vain and harmful. Christians have better spectacles in the beauty of God's creation and in the wonders recorded in Scripture, culminating in the devil lying conquered under Christ's feet.

outline.move: Novatian explains his joy at writing and his purpose: to admonish the faithful against spectacles, since some now give vice authority by twisting Scripture.
He reports and refutes the claim that Scripture permits spectacles because Elijah was a charioteer, David danced, and the apostle used athletic imagery.
He argues that biblical examples were meant to excite virtue, not permit spectacles, and that Scripture's silence on some matters is itself a prohibition.
He traces all spectacles to idolatry, their mother, and shows that attending them amounts to renouncing Christ and returning to the devil.
He describes the cruelty and vanity of circus games, and imagines interrogating an attendee who would confess to having passed through brothels on his way to the show.
He condemns the obscenity of the theater, where adultery and vice are taught publicly and effeminate performers enact ancient lusts.
He rejects musical and theatrical performances as vain and unfitting for Christians even apart from their dedication to idols.
He denounces combat sports and athletic contests as brutal, shameful, and corrupting to those who watch.
He offers the beauty of creation—sun, moon, stars, earth, sea, and living creatures—as the true spectacle for Christians.
He points to the wonders of Scripture and the defeat of the devil under Christ's feet as the most fitting spectacle, and closes with a blessing.

cast.name: Novatian
cast.who: The author, a Christian teacher writing to admonish the faithful.

cast.name: Elijah
cast.who: Old Testament prophet cited by opponents as a charioteer of Israel.

cast.name: David
cast.who: King of Israel cited by opponents for dancing before the ark.

cast.name: The unnamed apostle
cast.who: The apostle, not named by Novatian, whose athletic imagery opponents misuse to justify spectacles; the imagery matches Paul's epistles.

cast.name: Romulus
cast.who: Legendary founder of Rome who first consecrated circus games to Consus.

cast.name: Consus
cast.who: A Roman god to whom Romulus dedicated the first circus games.

cast.name: Ceres
cast.who: Roman goddess to whom scenic games were dedicated.

cast.name: Liber
cast.who: Roman god to whom scenic games were dedicated.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: The Lord whose body is dishonored by those who attend spectacles, and the Son of God the Father named in the closing doxology.

voices.speaker: Opponents (Christians defending spectacles)
voices.how_marked: Described in section 1 as 'bland and indulgent patrons of vices'; quoted directly in section 2 with 'inquiunt' ('they say')

key_terms.sense: Public shows—circus, theater, and athletic contests—that Christians are forbidden to attend.
Worship of idols, identified as the mother and origin of all public games.
The devil, portrayed as the artificer who mixed idolatry with spectacles to make it loved through pleasure.
A baptized believer, whose profession obliges avoidance of all indecent and idolatrous things.
Pleasure, especially the sensual pleasure of eyes and ears that draws people to spectacles.
Circus games, especially chariot racing, first consecrated by Romulus to Consus.
Scenic or theatrical games dedicated to Ceres and Liber, marked by obscene performances.
Contests, including Greek athletic competitions and combat sports, dedicated to various demons.
Demons, the presiding powers of the various Greek contests and all spectacles.
Evangelical virtue or excellence, which biblical examples are meant to excite in believers.
Vanity or emptiness, the character of spectacles even apart from their idolatrous origin.
Modesty or shame, which Scripture itself appeals to when it remains silent about forbidden things.
Brothel, used both literally for the route to the circus and figuratively for the theater as a brothel of public shame.
The consecrated body of Christ carried by a believer who hurries from church to the spectacle.
A legal-style objection or defense raised by opponents, here their claim that Scripture does not forbid spectacles.

scripture: Novatian cites Old Testament figures and events (Elijah, David, the parting of the sea, water from the rock, manna from heaven, the three youths in the furnace, Daniel among the lions) without formal book citations, and alludes to the apostle's athletic imagery in the epistles. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and Psalm numbering; where the Vulgate or LXX numbering differs, follow the modern English convention.
uncertain: The exact date of composition within Novatian's career.
The specific congregation or individuals addressed.
Whether the work was originally composed in Latin or translated from Greek.
Whether the unnamed 'apostolus' is Paul, though the athletic imagery matches his epistles.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Novatian writes because some Christians defend attending public spectacles by appealing to Scripture
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: non desunt uitiorum assertores blandi et indulgentes patroni qui praestant uitiis auctoritatem et quod est deterius censuram scripturarum caelestium in aduocationem criminum conuertunt, quasi sine culpa innocens spectaculorum ad remissionem animi appetatur uoluptas
_unresolved_facts.fix: Novatian writes because some Christians give authority to vices and twist the censure of heavenly Scriptures into advocacy for crimes, with spectacles as a particular example where this occurs

_unresolved_facts.claim: he aims to admonish those already instructed rather than instruct them anew
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: placuit paucis uos non nunc instruere, sed instructos admonere

_unresolved_facts.claim: He refutes appeals to biblical examples such as Elijah, David, and the unnamed apostle by showing these were written to stir virtue, not to permit spectacles
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Argumentum est ergo excitandae uirtutis, non permissio sine libertas spectandi gentilis erroris

_unresolved_facts.claim: He describes the immorality of the circus, theater, and athletic contests
He reports and refutes the claim that Scripture permits spectacles because Elijah was a charioteer, David danced, and the apostle used athletic imagery
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ubi', inquiunt, scripta sunt ista, ubi prohibita? alioquin et auriga est Israel Helias et ante aream Dauid ipse saltauit. nabla cynaras aera tympana tibias citharas choros legimus. apostolus quoque dimicans caestus et colluctationis nostrae aduersus spiritalia nequitiae proponit certamen. rursus cum de stadio sumit exempla, coronae quoque collocat praemia. cur ergo homini christiano fideli non liceat spectare quod licuit diuinis litteris scribare'?
_unresolved_facts.fix: He reports and refutes the opponents' claim that since Scripture records (not 'permits') these things—Elijah as charioteer, David dancing, musical instruments, and the apostle's athletic imagery—Christians may therefore spectate what Scripture was allowed to write about

_unresolved_facts.claim: He imagines interrogating an attendee who would confess to having passed through brothels on his way to the show
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: quem si rursus perrogem quo ad illud spectaculum itinere peruenerit, confitebitur per lupanarium, per prostitutarum nuda corpora, per lubricam libidinem, per dedecus publicum, per uulgarem lasciuiam, per communem omnium contumeliam
_unresolved_facts.fix: He imagines interrogating an attendee who would confess that he came to the spectacle by way of the brothel, through naked bodies of prostitutes, through slippery lust, through public disgrace, through common wantonness, through the shared insult of all

_unresolved_facts.claim: He rejects musical and theatrical performances as vain and unfitting for Christians even apart from their dedication to idols
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: haec etiam si non essent simulacris dicata, obeunda tamen et spectanda non essent christianis fidelibus

_unresolved_facts.claim: The unnamed apostle, whose athletic imagery opponents misuse to justify spectacles; the imagery matches Paul's epistles
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: apostolus quoque dimicans caestus et colluctationis nostrae aduersus spiritalia nequitiae proponit certamen. rursus cum de stadio sumit exempla, coronae quoque collocat praemia
_unresolved_facts.fix: The unnamed apostle, whose imagery of boxing, wrestling against spiritual wickedness, and racing for a crown opponents misuse to justify spectacles; the imagery matches Paul's epistles (1 Cor 9:24-27, Eph 6:12)

_unresolved_facts.claim: Described in section 1 as 'bland and indulgent patrons of vices'; quoted directly in section 2 with 'inquiunt' ('they say')
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: non desunt uitiorum assertores blandi et indulgentes patroni... 'ubi', inquiunt
